title: Results Come in for Midterms That Will Shape Rest of Trump’s Presidency
author: TIME Staff
body:
Here’s what to know

- Polls have closed nationwide except in Alaska.

- Democrats flipped key Senate seats in Iowa, Kansas, North Carolina, South Carolina, and Texas.

- Democrat Chris Pappas has defeated former Republican Sen. John Sununu in New Hampshire, becoming the first openly gay man elected to the Senate. Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms also won in the Georgia gubernatorial race, becoming the first Black woman elected governor of any state.

Trump rages against blue wave

Nov 4, 12:15 AM

The President railed against Democrats' victories in the midterms on Tuesday evening in a series of Truth Social posts.

Shortly before midnight, Trump posted a photo of a red hat reminiscent of the ones often worn by MAGA supporters and by the President himself—but this one had the word "Veto" printed on it. The image appears to be a threat that the President will use his veto power against the House and the Senate, the latter of which AP called for Democrats on Tuesday evening. AP has not yet called control of the House, but other news outlets have projected that Democrats will win the majority in the lower chamber as well.

In another social media post, Trump levied an attack against Texas Gov. Greg Abbott, who lost his re-election bid to Democratic candidate Gina Hinojosa on Tuesday evening—a stunning result in a state that has not elected a Democrat governor since 1990.

Trump had endorsed Abbott in the race. But after Abbott's loss on Tuesday, the President accused the Texas governor of being a "RINO," which stands for "Republican In Name Only."

"If Greg Abbott, the Governor of Texas, hadn’t become a RINO in the last six months of his Political Life, he wouldn’t have lost," Trump said in a Truth Social post. "He went back to his original formula, and it wasn’t pretty!"

A few minutes later, the President posted again, saying, "I’m going to become a Political Pundit, both good and bad, on the reasons these Candidates won and lost!" — Chantelle Lee

Democrats have won the Senate, AP calls

Nov 4, 12:00 AM

AP called the Senate for Democrats shortly before midnight, in a stunning rebuke of the Trump Administration and the Republican Party.

As of Tuesday evening, AP has called 51 seats in the upper chamber for Democrats and 39 for Republicans. AP has yet to call 10 races for the upper chamber. The news outlet hasn’t yet called the House majority for Democrats, but others, including CNN, have projected that Democrats will win control of the lower chamber. Democrats capturing both chambers of Congress would mark only the fifth time since World War II that a political party was able to flip both the Senate and the House in a midterm election. — Chantelle Lee

Read the full story here.

House Democrats celebrate election gains

Nov 3, 11:50 PM

House Democrats are rejoicing over their election victories, including projections from CNN and NBC that they have regained control of the chamber. The AP has not yet called the majority.

In Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries’ election-night headquarters just south of the Capitol, a crowd of roughly 100 people erupted in cheers when CNN announced the projection. Supporters broke into chants of “Jeffries! Jeffries! Jeffries!”

Rep. Suzan DelBene of Washington state, who chairs the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said in the headquarters: “The American people have spoken decisively all across the country. They have had enough of the broken promises from house Republicans, and they are ready for new leadership in Congress, and they're going to get it.” — Chad de Guzman with reporting contributed by Nik Popli

Democrat Josh Turek wins key Senate pick-up in Iowa

Nov 3, 11:45 PM

Democratic state representative Josh Turek has been elected as U.S. Senator for Iowa, the AP called, beating Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson to take the seat to be vacated by GOP Sen. Joni Ernst, who is retiring after two terms.

Turek, a paralympian gold medalist, is the first Democrat Iowa has sent to the Senate since Tom Harkin was re-elected in 2008. — Chad de Guzman

House Democratic Leader hails ‘great American comeback’

Nov 3, 11:40 PM

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries hailed a "great American comeback" in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday night after several outlets projected that Democrats had won back the lower chamber.

"America is back...I learned very early on that a setback was nothing more than a setup for a comeback. Today begins the great American comeback," he said. "This is not a partisan moment. This is a patriotic one. This is not a blue moment or a red moment. It's a red, white, and blue moment because America has won tonight." — Connor Greene

Adam Hamilton becomes first Kansas Democrat elected to Senate in nearly a century

Nov 3, 11:35 PM

For the first time since 1932, voters in Kansas have elected a Democrat to the U.S. Senate.

Democrat Adam Hamilton, a United Methodist pastor, has won the Senate race, AP called on Tuesday evening, defeating the Republican incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall. Marshall, who had been seeking a second term, had been backed by the President. He is among several GOP Senate candidates, including Sen. Darline Graham, who received Trump's endorsement in this midterm cycle—but were still toppled by their Democratic opponents on Tuesday evening.

Read the full story here. — Chantelle Lee

Texas Governor Greg Abbott loses to Democrat Gina Hinojosa

Nov 3, 11:25 PM

Texas Governor Greg Abbott has been defeated by Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, the AP has called.

Abbott’s stunning defeat marks the end of a long streak of Republican governorship since 1995, including George W. Bush who governed Texas from 1995 to 2000 before becoming President.

Abbott, who has been governor of Texas for three terms, previously spent more than two decades in the Texas judicial system. In 1995, then-Governor Bush appointed Abbott to the Texas Supreme Court. He was then re-elected twice in the late 90s. In 2014, he ran for Texas governor and won by more than 20 points against state senator Wendy Davis. — Philip Wang

Democrat James Talarico flips Texas Senate seat

Nov 3, 11:10 PM

John Cornyn, the outgoing Republican senior Senator for Texas, congratulated Democratic candidate James Talarico, the state representative who defeated GOP nominee Ken Paxton for Cornyn’s seat.

“The voters have spoken, and I want to extend my congratulations to James Talarico on his election to the U.S. Senate,” Cornyn posted on X, before the AP had called the race, though it did less than an hour later. “I look forward to meeting him and offering my assistance with his transition as he prepares to serve Texans in the U.S. Senate.”

Talarico is the first Democrat to win a statewide race in Texas since 1994 and is also the first Democrat to be elected Senator by Texans since 1988. — Chad de Guzman

Read the full story here.

Trump tells Times that he will accept election results

Nov 3, 11:05 PM

The President told the New York Times on Election Night that he will accept the results of the midterms.

"I am absolutely willing to accept those results," he told the news outlet. "We’ll work with the Democrats, and we’ll, you know, look forward to working with them. We’ll probably work something out." — Chantelle Lee

All 48 states in the contiguous U.S. close, leaving Alaska and Hawaii polls still open

Nov 3, 11:00 PM

Polls in California, Idaho, Oregon, and Washington have closed, leaving only those outside of the contiguous U.S. in Alaska and Hawaii.

California’s 22nd district, a toss up race between incumbent Republican Rep. David Valadao and Democrat Randy Villegas, presents a pick-up opportunity for Democrats. The state’s 48 district is also leaning towards Democrats flipping an open Republican-held seat.

Oregon’s gubernatorial race, where Tina Kotek seeks reelection, is also a competitive race, and leans Democratic. — Connor Greene

Democrat Amy Acton wins Ohio governor’s race

Nov 3, 10:55 PM

Democratic candidate Dr. Amy Acton will be Ohio’s next governor, the AP called, defeating the Trump-backed Republican Vivek Ramaswamy in a heated race.

The race entered the national spotlight in the lead-up to Election Day after Ramaswamy’s campaign released a controversial attack ad against Acton that featured her estranged mother. While the President and Vice President defended Ramaswamy amid backlash generated by the ad, other members of the Republican Party slammed the campaign for the move.

Acton’s win is a stunning result in a state that has not elected a Democrat to the governor’s residence in 20 years.

Read the full story here. — Chantelle Lee

Trump rails against election results

Nov 3, 10:50 PM

The President seemed to express his frustration with the results coming in on Election Night.

"I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!" he said in a Truth Social post.

The midterms have largely been viewed as a referendum on Trump’s presidency, which faces record-low approval ratings. — Chantelle Lee

Democrat Annie Andrews flips South Carolina Senate seat in stunning upset

Nov 3, 10:45 PM

In South Carolina, Democratic Dr. Annie Andrews will defeat Republican Sen. Darline Graham for a seat in the U.S. Senate race, the AP has called—a stunning upset in a staunchly red state that has not elected a Democrat to the upper chamber this century.

The race for the seat, was upended after longtime Sen. Lindsey Graham died unexpectedly in July. His sister, Darline Graham, was appointed by the South Carolina governor to finish out the rest of her brother's term. At the urging of the President, Darline Graham later announced her intention to run for a full term in the midterms.

But polls leading up to Election Day showed that the race was a much closer fight than it was before Lindsey Graham's death, when he was running for re-election. Andrews, a pediatrician, received widespread support from the Democratic party and even secured bipartisan endorsements, while Darline Graham faced criticisms from within her own party over her minimal political background.

Read the full story here. — Chantelle Lee

Voters in Virginia pass abortion rights amendment

Nov 3, 10:15 PM

Voters in Virginia passed an amendment to the state’s constitution that creates multiple protections for reproductive health.

The amendment constitutionally protects abortions taking place during the first two trimesters of pregnancy and provides protections for pregnant women’s health later in their pregnancies, among other rights regarding fertility health.

“Every individual has the fundamental right to reproductive freedom,” the amendment says, including decisions related to “prenatal care, childbirth, postpartum care, contraception, abortion care, miscarriage management, and fertility care.”

Two other abortion rights protection measures are on the ballots in Idaho and Nevada, while another measure in Missouri would repeal abortion rights protections voted for in 2024. — Connor Greene

Polls begin to close in the West

Nov 3, 10:00 PM

Polls have closed in Montana, Nevada, and Utah, with some but not yet all in Idaho and Oregon.

Montana and Nevada are home to closely watched House races. Republican Aaron Flint is facing off against Democrat Sam Forstag in Montana’s first district, where Democrats have a chance to flip a seat being vacated by Republican Ryan Zinke in a race deemed a toss up. In Nevada’s second district, Republican David Flippo and Democrat Teresa Benitez-Thompson are competing for retiring Republican Rep. Mark Amodei’s position in a race favoring Republicans.

Also in Nevada, Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo faces Democratic Attorney General Aaron Ford in a toss up. Lombardo had come under fire during his campaign after video showed him using his name in a traffic stop before being let go without a ticket. — Connor Greene

New polls show major shift to Democrats among young voters, Latinos

Nov 3, 9:45 PM

New polls conducted in all 50 states show that the Democratic Party is expanding its lead among young voters and Latino voters.

The polls, conducted by SSRS in partnership with a consortium of media outlets, show a sharp Democratic shift among young voters: 71% of those ages 18 to 29 identify as Democrats, compared with 25% as Republicans. In 2024, Democrats led Republicans among that age group by 54% to 43%.

Latino voters have also shifted toward Democrats, with 60% identifying as Democrats and 35% as Republicans. That 25-point advantage is up from a five-point lead in 2024, when the split was 51% to 46%.

The poll surveyed more than 100,000 at voting locations, online, and by telephone. — Philip Wang

Keisha Lance Bottoms elected governor of Georgia

Nov 3, 9:30 PM

Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms has won the Georgia gubernatorial race, beating Republican billionaire Rick Jackson to replace the term-limited GOP Gov. Brian Kemp.

The Associated Press called the race at 9:24 p.m. ET. Bottoms’ victory also flips the state, marking the first time Georgia has had a Democratic governor since 2003.

A former mayor of Atlanta and a former Biden Administration official, Bottoms’ election makes her the state’s first Black and first female governor, as well as the U.S.’s first Black female governor. — Chad de Guzman

Several more polls close in the final hours of Election Day

Nov 3, 9:00 PM

The latest polls have now closed in Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, North Dakota, South Dakota, Texas, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.

Iowa marks another key Senate race to replace outgoing Republican Sen. Joni Ernst. In one of the tightest races this midterm cycle, Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson, a former broadcast journalist, is facing off against Democratic state Rep. Josh Turek, a paralympic gold medalist.

Trump won Iowa by 13 points in 2024, but the race is considered a toss up.

Other key Senate races are taking place in Nebraska, which leans Republican, and in Minnesota, which leans Democratic. — Connor Greene

Republican Ashley Moody secures full Senate term in Florida, defeating state Rep. Angie Nixon

Nov 3, 8:58 PM

Incumbent Republican Sen. Ashley Moody has defeated democratic socialist state Rep. Angie Nixon in Florida’s special Senate election.

The Associated Press called the race for Moody, who entered the Senate last year after being appointed by Gov. Ron DeSantis to replace Secretary of State Marco Rubio when he left the position to join the Trump Administration in Washington.

Moody was forecasted to win by the Cook Political Report, which categorized the race as “likely Republican.”

Nixon had called for Moody to be arrested during the campaign over accusations that she mishandled taxpayer funds as the state’s attorney general. Moody has denied wrongdoing. — Connor Green

Florida Democrats win in two House districts redrawn in Republicans’ favor

Nov 3, 8:43 PM

Two Florida Democrats have won in House districts that were recently redrawn in Republicans’ favor, The Associated Press has called.

Rep. Kathy Castor has won more than 51% of the vote, with 97% of votes counted by Tuesday evening, AP reported, successfully securing an 11th term in Florida’s 14th District. Republican Mike Beltran, who was previously a state legislator and attorney, has earned less than 46% of the vote.

Rep. Jared Moskowitz has won more than 51% of the vote in Florida’s 25th District, defeating his Republican opponent Scott Singer, a previous mayor of Boca Raton who earned less than 47% of the vote, AP reported, with 96% of the vote counted. Moskowitz currently represents the 23rd Congressional District in the House. — Chantelle Lee

Democrat Roy Cooper flips Senate seat in North Carolina

Nov 3, 8:37 PM

Democrat Roy Cooper has flipped a key Senate seat in North Carolina, defeating Republican Michael Whatley to claim the open seat being vacated by Republican Sen. Thom Tillis.

Cooper's win marks a key pick up for his party in its fight to wrest back control of the upper chamber from Republicans.

Cooper, a former governor and state attorney general, will succeed Tillis, who decided not to seek reelection.

The Associated Press called the race just after 8:20 p.m. EST. — Connor Greene

Polls close in Arkansas

Nov 3, 8:30 PM

Polls have closed in Arkansas, with more—but not yet all—also now closed in Kansas, Michigan, North Dakota, South Dakota, and Texas.

In Arkansas, a solid red state, Republicans are favored in every congressional and gubernatorial race. The Cook Political Report ranks all races across the Senate and House, as well as the contest for Governor, as “solid Republican,” among the seats it deems least likely to flip, with the exception of one ranked as “likely Republican” in the state’s second district. — Connor Greene

Chris Pappas wins in New Hampshire, becomes first openly gay man elected to the U.S. Senate

Nov 3, 8:29 PM

Four-term Rep. Chris Pappas has become the first openly gay man to be elected in to the U.S. Senate after defeating former Sen. John Sununu in New Hampshire.

The Associated Press called the race for Pappas, whose opponent is a well-known name in the state. Sununu’s brother served as governor until last year and his father was also governor.

New Hampshire marked another possible opportunity for Republicans to pick up an open seat, that of long-time Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen. — Connor Greene

Voting is still underway, with sporadic technical glitches

Nov 3, 8:10 PM

Most polls on the East Coast have closed. Throughout the day, there have been sporadic reports of technical difficulties, but the Election Day vote has been running smoothly by and large.

Election officials in Fulton County, Georgia, said that more than 1,000 ballots cast in Fulton County may need to be rescanned as a result of two ballot scanners malfunctioning. Secretary of State Brad Raffensperger said that the scanner issues would not delay election results.

Polls will close at 9 p.m. as scheduled in Westchester County, New York, where a technical failure has led to polling stations across the county to switch to emergency ballots. The tabulation will be delayed because of this failure, which will affect a close-fought House race. — Philip Wang

Democrat Jon Ossoff wins re-election in Georgia

Nov 3, 8:02 PM

Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff has won reelection in Georgia against Republican Rep. Mike Collins, in another victory for Democrats in their effort to win back control the upper chamber.

The Associated Press called the race less than an hour after polls closed in the state on Tuesday.

Georgia marked a potential opportunity for Republicans to pick up a Senate seat in a state that Trump won by a slim margin in 2024. Ossoff consistently led in polling leading up to Election Day, however, and also had a serious cash advantage over his opponent throughout the campaign. — Connor Greene

Polls close in several key toss-up races

Nov 3, 8:00 PM

Polls have closed in several more pivotal battleground races, including in Maine, Kansas, Texas, Michigan, New Hampshire, Pennsylvania, and more.

In perhaps the most closely watched midterm contest, James Talarico, who is vying to become Texas’ first Democratic Senator since 1993, is facing off against Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton in a toss-up race.

Another tight race in the state’s fifteenth district is testing the GOP’s support among Hispanic voters, with whom Trump made gains in the 2024 presidential election. Republican Monica De La Cruz, who flipped the district in 2022, is seeking to keep her seat against Democrat Bobby Pulido, a popular Latin Grammy-winning Tejano musician.

Other toss-up races are playing out in Kansas, where incumbent Sen. Roger Marshall is defending his seat against Democrat Adam Hamilton, and Maine, where Republican Sen. Susan Collins is seeking her sixth term. Collin’s opponent, Democrat Troy Jackson, became the party’s nominee after Graham Platner, who won the primary, dropped out of the race amid sexual assault allegations, which he has denied.

Michigan’s Senate race is also closely watched, with the Cook Political Report rating it as “lean Democratic” in favor of progressive Abdul El-Sayed, who is facing off against Republican Mike Rogers.

In Michigan’s seventh district, meanwhile, Republican Rep. Tom Barrett is facing off against progressive William Lawrence in a toss-up race that ranks as one of the most expensive House races in the country.

Another toss-up is taking place in Pennsylvania’s first district, where incumbent Republican Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick is going head-to-head with Democrat Bob Harvie. — Connor Greene

Democrats notch the night's first Senate win

Nov 3, 7:42 PM

Democratic Virginia Sen. Mark Warner has been reelected to a fourth term, defeating Republican challenger Bert Mizusawa.

The AP called the race for Warner, whose seat was considered among the safest in the country this midterm cycle, just minutes after polls closed in Virginia at 7 p.m. EST. It marked the first call of the night in the closely watched battle for control of the Senate.

Votes are now being counted in multiple states with more tightly contested Senate races where polls have closed, including Georgia, North Carolina, Ohio, and South Carolina. — Annika Neklason

Polls close in Ohio and North Carolina, home to multiple closely watched congressional races

Nov 3, 7:30 PM

Polls have closed in Ohio and West Virginia. Most polls have also closed in North Carolina, where some precincts received an extension due to minor technical issues at certain localities.

Ohio and North Carolina are home to a handful of closely watched Senate and House races.

In an Ohio toss-up, former Democratic Sen. Sherrod Brown is seeking to unseat Republican Sen. Jon Husted, who was appointed by Republican Gov. Mike DeWine to replace Vice President JD Vance when Vance went to the White House in 2025. North Carolina is now ranked “likely Democrat” by the Cook Political Report in what was considered a much more competitive race before Republicans pulled out to focus on other contests.

In Ohio’s seventh district, meanwhile, Democrat Brian Poindexter could have a chance to flip incumbent Republican Rep. Max Miller’s seat. The race has received outsized national attention amid domestic abuse allegations against Miller, who has denied all wrongdoing.

A House toss-up is also playing out in North Carolina’s first district, where incumbent Democratic Rep. Don Davis is being challenged by Laurie Buckhout, who he beat by only a slim margin in 2024. — Connor Greene

More polls close across the country, including in battleground states

Nov 3, 7:00 PM

All polls have now closed in Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, South Carolina, Vermont, and Virginia, while some have closed in Florida and New Hampshire. In some of those states, key races could help determine which party will control the House and the Senate.

In deep-red South Carolina, Darline Graham, the sister of late Republican Sen. Lindsey Graham, is running against Annie Andrews in a Senate race The Cook Political Report ranks as “lean Republican,” just one step removed from a toss-up. In another closely watched Senate race, incumbent Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff is facing Republican Mike Collins in Georgia, which has been rated “likely Democratic.”

A handful of toss-up House races are also playing out in some of those states, including in Virginia and South Carolina’s first districts and Florida’s fourteenth.

In Virginia’s first district, Democrat Shannon Taylor has the chance to oust a longtime Republican incumbent, Rep. Rob Wittman. An open Republican-held seat is meanwhile up for grabs in South Carolina’s first district, which is being vacated by Rep. Nancy Mace. Republican Jenny Costa Honeycutt and Democrat Nancy Lacore are vying for the spot. And in Florida’s fourteenth district, incumbent Democrat Rep. Kathy Castor is fighting to retain her seat against Republican Mike Beltran after new electoral maps changed the district’s composition.

More polls are expected to close every half hour until 9 p.m. EST, and then every hour until 1 a.m. — Connor Greene

FBI debunks claims of “fraudulent ballot seizure” in Houston

Nov 3, 6:21 PM

The FBI on Tuesday debunked a claim that it has uncovered more than 20,000 fraudulent ballots in favor of Democratic candidates at a warehouse in Houston, Texas, on Monday night.

In a statement, the FBI said no election-related operation occurred in Houston and that information is false.

The unproven claim of an raid first began to surface on Tuesday afternoon and was quickly shared among conservative online users. The post also features three photos purported to show the scene of raid. Fact-checking outlet PolitiFact reported that the three images were taken in three different states and none of them were related to a FBI raid in Houston. — Philip Wang

Heading into the midterms, Trump's approval rating dropped to a historic low

Nov 3, 6:17 PM

President Donald Trump’s approval rating reached a historic low in the weeks leading up to Election Day: According to the Pew Research Center, his approval rating dropped to 30% at the beginning of October. The last time a sitting President’s approval rating fell to a comparable level that close to a midterm election was when Harry Truman was in the Oval Office in 1946.

Surveys show that the public’s dissatisfaction with the President stems largely from the economy; about 26% of adults in the country approve of how Trump has been dealing with the issue, according to polling from The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research last month. And the Pew Research Center’s survey revealed that 84% of registered voters felt that the economy was a “very important issue” for them in this election.

Midterms already tend to be difficult for the party in control of the White House, which historically loses seats in these elections. But political experts have told TIME that this year’s midterms are an especially challenging environment for Republicans. Many generic ballot polls have indicated that voters backed Democrats over Republicans heading into Tuesday's elections, and even polling in deep red states has suggested that GOP candidates have experienced trouble keeping leads over their Democratic opponents.

“I think we can expect Republicans to be facing an uphill battle at the polls,” Costas Panagopoulos, a professor of political science at Northeastern University, previously told TIME. “We can expect that they will likely lose seats in the House and also the Senate. And the question is will they lose enough seats to lose the majority in either or both those chambers. That is entirely within the realm of possibility. And that has to do both with Trump’s relatively low approval rating, historically speaking, but also the constellation of candidates in the mix.”

Read the full story here. — Chantelle Lee

First polls close in parts of Kentucky and Indiana

Nov 3, 6:00 PM

The first polls of the 2026 midterm elections have closed in parts of Kentucky and Indiana.

In a couple districts in those areas, tight House races could provide initial glimpses into how Democrats and Republicans are faring in the fight for Congress. The Cook Political Report rates Kentucky’s sixth district, where Republican Ralph Alvarado faces off against Democrat Zach Dembo, a toss-up. And in a race considered slightly less close, it ranks Indiana’s fifth district, where Democrat JD Ford is challenging incumbent Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz, lean Republican.

Polls across the rest of the country will close in the coming hours. At 7 p.m., polls will close in Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, South Carolina, Vermont, Virginia, Florida, and New Hampshire. — Connor Greene

What time do the polls close—and when will we know the election results?

Nov 3, 5:27 PM

Most polls around the country close around 7 p.m. or 8 p.m. local time. Because the U.S. is divided across several time zones, however, those closures are spread over several hours on Election Day.

Here is when the latest polls close in each of the 50 states and Washington, D.C., in Eastern Standard Time.

- 7 p.m. EST: Georgia, Indiana, Kentucky, South Carolina, Vermont, and Virginia.

- 7:30 p.m. EST: Ohio and West Virginia. North Carolina also typically closes its final polls at this time, but due to minor technical issues reported in some localities on Tuesday—which have since been resolved—the state’s board of elections has extended voting hours in some precincts.

- 8 p.m. EST: Alabama, Connecticut, Delaware, Florida, Illinois, Maine, Maryland, Massachusetts, Mississippi, Missouri, New Hampshire, New Jersey, Oklahoma, Rhode Island, Tennessee, and Washington, D.C. In Pennsylvania, most polling sites will close at 8 p.m., but in three precincts they will stay open for an additional half hour “due to machine set-up issues” that delayed the opening of those polls this morning, according to Chester County officials.

- 8:30 p.m. EST: Arkansas.

- 9 p.m. EST: Arizona, Colorado, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Michigan, Minnesota, Nebraska, New Mexico, New York, North Dakota, South Dakota, Texas, Wisconsin, and Wyoming.

- 10 p.m. EST: Montana, Nevada, and Utah.

- 11 p.m. EST: California, Idaho, Oregon, and Washington state.

- Midnight EST: Hawaii.

- 1 a.m. EST: Alaska

Some races are likely to be called on Tuesday night, while in other, tighter contests it could take multiple days—if not longer—to determine a winner. It all comes down to the states, which the U.S. Constitution empowers to establish the times, places, and manners of holding elections and counting ballots.

“There are all these differences, both in process and deadlines, and geography, and who the voters are, and who the candidates are, that make a difference in what this looks like,” Mitchell Brown, a professor of political science at Auburn University and the author of “How We Vote: Innovations in American Elections,” tells TIME.

Read the full story here. — Connor Greene

Candidates in toss-up House race urge calm after ballot scanner failures in Westchester County, New York

Nov 3, 5:24 PM

Republican Rep. Mike Lawler of New York and Democrat Cait Conley, who are facing off in a close-fought House race, have both called on Tuesday for voters to stay in line after ballot scanners failed at polling locations in Westchester County, New York.

During a press conference, Lawler said both parties are working with the county and New York State board of elections to come to a solution.

“Do not leave the polling place without voting,” Lawler added. “Every vote is going to be counted, and is going to be counted tonight.”

Conley also addressed the technical issues at polling locations in a social media post and said, “don't be dissuaded and have your voice heard.”

According to New York State Board of Elections, because the ballot scanners across Westchester County are unable to scan ballots immediately, the ballots need to be temporarily placed in orange bags which will be transported by local police to a secure location. The ballots will then be scanned under supervision of attorneys from both sides and it will take several hours to scan them all in, which could delay the results of a competitive congressional district. County Executive Ken Jenkins said the machines were not hacked and there was nothing of that nature wrong with the voting process. — Philip Wang

ICE threatens arrests over illegal voting, drawing rebuke from Newsom

Nov 3, 4:45 PM

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) on Tuesday threatened to arrest people who vote illegally in the midterms.

“If you vote illegally, we will find you. We will track you down, arrest you, and prosecute you,” the agency wrote on X. “There will be no escape.”

The post quickly drew a rebuke from California Gov. Gavin Newsom, who threw the same threats back at the agency, echoing the agency’s language: “If YOU show up to the polls illegally, we will find you. We will track you down, arrest you, and prosecute you. There will be no escape.”

Newsom in a later post issued another warning to “DONALD TRUMP’S THUGS: If you violate California’s laws, if you interfere with the vote, you will be prosecuted.”

Trump last month threatened California election officials with jail time amid his administration’s push to set aside ballots from voters it identified as possible noncitizens.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin also said Tuesday that “only American citizens should be deciding American elections.” The Department of Justice and Homeland Security Investigations added to the chorus, touting arrests of people accused of voting illegally.

The comments fall in line with Trump’s repeated claims of widespread noncitizen voting, though research has found it to be exceedingly rare. — Connor Greene

DOJ can continue asking states to set aside mail-in ballots, appeals court rules

Nov 3, 4:14 PM

A federal appeals court on Tuesday made a stunning reversal and allowed the Department of Justice to continue its pressure campaign telling state governments to not count mail-in ballots from noncitizens.

In a 6-5 decision, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that the Trump Administration can continue asking state election officials to set aside from voters it identified as possible noncitizens. It also said the DOJ can continue warning state election officials that knowingly counting unlawful ballots could result in federal prosecution.

On Monday, the same appeals court blocked the move.

The court's decision, which is separate from the legal saga between the DOJ and the state of California, will not affect states’ tabulation and certification processes, given that states are not legally required to comply with the department’s request, according to Jonathan Diaz, the Director of Voting Advocacy and Partnerships at Campaign Legal Center. — Philip Wang

Oklahoma man charged with mailing white powder to public officials

Nov 3, 4:14 PM

An Oklahoma City resident faces charges of conveying false or misleading information and hoaxes and mailing threatening communications, according to court documents unsealed Tuesday in the U.S. District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma.

The unsealed records show that Robin Martin was arrested Monday for allegedly sending threatening letters containing white powder ahead of the 2024 and 2026 elections, with investigators linking more than 700 mailings to him this fall alone.

According to the court filings, the white powder that has been tested so far was determined to be nonhazardous—likely either yeast or flour—but the accompanying messages included references to treason. One envelope back in 2024 had the return address of “U.S.T.E.A., United States Traitor Elimination Army, Takoma Park, MD.”

The affidavit alleges that in 2024, Martin “described perceived issues with the 2020 election” in his letters, claiming “that President Donald Trump won the 2020 election, and voiced concerns regarding some of the same issues recurring in the then-upcoming 2024 election.”

The letters also threatened election officials, including one that told the Oklahoma State Election Board to “stay on the right side of history your life might depend on it!”

The arrest comes less than a month after the FBI announced its investigation into letters with “suspicious substances” that had been mailed to congressional and election offices. In October, NBC News reported state election offices in Louisiana, Ohio, and Oklahoma were sent packages containing mysterious powders.

Martin was expected to make an appearance in the U.S. District Court in Oklahoma City on Tuesday. — Rebecca Schneid

Political heavyweights make final push to turn out voters

Nov 3, 4:02 PM

Soon after the U.S. and Israel first launched an aerial attack on Iran on Feb. 28, Iran’s leadership restricted access to the Strait of Hormuz, the waterway through which roughly one-fifth of the world’s oil once passed.

Americans saw a similar spike when Russia invaded Ukraine and sent gas prices soaring to $5.02 per gallon in June 2022. By Election Day that year, however, gas had dropped down to an average of around $3.80 per gallon.

Republicans worry that high prices at the pump could translate to voter frustration. A Pew Research Center study released in early October found that 74% of U.S. adults were very concerned about gasoline and energy prices, up more than 30% from January.

Lowering costs was one of Trump’s major campaign promises when he ran for a second term in 2024. In the weeks leading up to the midterms, he has homed in on fuel prices. In early October, he pushed for the Group of Seven countries to release 100 million barrels of oil and fuel products in the coming months; he signed an executive order on Oct. 5 to temporarily permit highway use of red-dyed diesel; and on Oct. 13, he announced a surprise agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to supply millions of tons of Russian diesel to U.S. and global markets.

What time do polls open across the U.S.?

Nov 3, 3:45 AM

Election Day is underway, and polling precincts are set to open nationwide for in-person voting to add to the more than 58 million early votes already cast for the 2026 midterm elections that will decide the control of Congress for the final two years of Donald Trump’s presidency as well as numerous state and local contests.

Polling place hours vary by state, but commonly follow a 7 a.m. to 7 p.m. local time schedule. The opening schedules of the following states differ (indicated in local times):

- 6 a.m.: Arizona, Connecticut, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, some parts of Maine, Missouri, New Jersey, New York, and Virginia.

- 6:30 a.m.: North Carolina, Ohio, and West Virginia.

- 7:30 a.m.: Arkansas

- 8 a.m.: Idaho, though counties may open elections at 7 a.m. local time; parts of Nebraska that are under Central Time

There are also some in-state variations.

- In Kansas, polling places must open by 7 a.m, but state law also allows counties to open polling locations as early as 6 a.m.

- In Maine, polls generally open between 6 and 8 a.m., but towns with fewer than 500 residents may open as late as 10 a.m.

- In Massachusetts, polls may open as early as 5:45 a.m. and no later than 7 a.m.

- While Minnesota polls open at 7 a.m., qualifying small towns may open as late as 10 a.m.

- In Montana, most polling places must open by 7 a.m., but towns with fewer than 400 electors may open as late as 12 p.m.

- In New Hampshire, municipalities decide on poll opening times, as long as it’s before 11 a.m.

- In North Dakota, polling precincts must open by 9 a.m. and no earlier than 7 a.m.

- Polling centers across most of Rhode Island open at 7 a.m., with the exception of New Shoreham Town Hall, where they open at 9 a.m.

- In Tennessee, counties decide what time—between 7 a.m. and 9 a.m.—the polls will open.

- And in Vermont, the polls may open as early as 5 a.m. and as late as 10 a.m.

- Oregon and Washington primarily vote by mail.

Voters may find their polling place by contacting their state or local election office here or checking their voter registration here.
